string-array.name: home_xtc_info
string-array.item: Why phone stereo sounds narrow

The two phone speakers are about 15 cm apart. The left speaker does not only reach your left ear: its sound bends around your head and reaches the right ear almost as loud. The same goes for the right speaker. This leak to the other ear is called crosstalk.\n\nWith both ears hearing nearly the same thing, your brain places the sound in a small spot in the middle of the phone. A song that spreads wide on earphones gathers into the centre on the phone.
Cancelling the leak in advance

Spatial (XTC, crosstalk cancellation) sends an upside-down copy of the leak from the other speaker. Just as the left speaker reaches the right ear, the right speaker plays the same sound inverted and a little later, and the two cancel near the right ear.\n\nThat inverted sound leaks to the left ear too, so another one cancels it, and so on. The calculation repeats, each round weaker, and dies away quickly.
Where the idea comes from

It goes back to Atal and Schroeder at Bell Labs in the 1960s. Rootnote builds on RACE, which Ralph Glasgal published in 2007: two loudspeakers placed close together, seen at nearly the same angle as a phone at 30-50 cm.\n\nCommercial systems such as Dolby Atmos do similar things on phone speakers. Rootnote uses only published methods and its own code.
Why it asks for distance and head size

To cancel well, the inverted sound has to come at the right moment. The left speaker reaches the right ear about 0.1 ms after the left ear, and that time depends on the distance to the phone and the size of your head.\n\nNo need to measure your head: a standard head (hat about 57 cm) is the default, and small / medium / large by hat size is enough. The distance matters much more than the head size.
Where it sounds best

The inverted sound has to meet the leak right at your ears, so the best spot is small. Hold the phone sideways with your face in front of the screen. Turning your head or tilting the phone only weakens the effect; it does not break the sound.
It leaves the bass alone

Low notes have long wavelengths; cancelling them would need a lot of boost, which strains the speakers and fights the virtual bass. So spatial works only from about 400 Hz to 8 kHz, where voices and instruments get their place. Virtual bass and spatial each look after their own range.
Presets

Subtle: only the parts that differ left and right, so the vocals in the centre keep their tone.\nBalanced: the centre too, so it gets wider; the vocals change a little.\nClear: the strongest. In the right spot the sound spreads out to beside your ears.
Held upright

Upright, the two speakers sit above each other instead of left and right. Both then reach both ears almost equally, so there is no leak to cancel, and spatial does not work.\n\nYou can choose instead (advanced settings, Held upright): leave it and only spatial switches off, stereo as it is; mono plays the same sound from both; two-way lets the bottom speaker take the bass and the top one the highs, so the two no longer play the same highs from two heights and the small top speaker is spared the bass. It changes after a second upright, and spatial comes back when you turn the phone sideways.
Honest limits

How much less the sides blend is calculated with a computer model (about 3-10 dB in the mid range). Ears and heads differ, so the feel differs too. Videos and calls with everything in the centre change little.\n\nIt switches off by itself on earphones or Bluetooth and during blind comparisons and measurements.

string-array.name: story_scene_a11y
string-array.item: Seen from above. Sound waves from the phone\'s left and right speakers reach both ears, and the sound gathers into one point in the middle of the phone.
On its way from the left speaker to the right ear, the right speaker sends an inverted wave. Added together, the two waves make a flat line.
Two loudspeakers far away move in and become the phone, seen from the head at the same angle. Below, a timeline: the 1960s, 2007, Rootnote.
Change the distance to the phone and the head size. The numbers below show the angle and how much later the sound arrives.
The best spot glows in front of the face. As the head moves sideways the lines misalign and the glow fades, but the sound stays.
On a strip from 20 Hz to 20 kHz, below 400 Hz is teal (virtual bass) and 400 Hz to 8 kHz is purple (spatial).
Choosing a preset changes how far the centre dot (vocals) and the side dots (instruments) spread.
The phone held upright, seen from the front. Both speakers are as far from either ear; then thick bass waves spread from the bottom speaker and fine treble waves from the top one.
Spatial turns on and off, and the side dots spread and close.

resources.string: Not set yet. If the sound leans to one ear, even them out.
The phone\'s top and bottom speakers differ in size and sound. Spatial assumes they are the same, so a big difference pulls the sound to one ear. Evened out here, spatial keeps the centre.
